title: Deposition of Cu on CNT to synthesize electrocatalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2: advantages of supercritical fluid deposition technique
abstract: One of the most promising technologies for the mitigation of CO2 emissions involves its electrocatalytic reduction to valuable products. However, the development of effective catalysts is still a challenge. In this work, three different techniques have been compared for the synthesis of catalysts involving Cu-based nanoparticles deposited on carbon nanotubes (Cu/CNT): precipitation, microemulsion and supercritical fluid deposition (SFD). According to XRD, SFD allows obtaining mainly copper nanoparticles, while copper oxides are obtained by precipitation. Crystallite size of predominant Cu species of catalysts are between 7 (microemulsion) and 16 nm (SFD). The use of these catalysts in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in gas phase produce carbon monoxide as main CO2 reduction product, followed by formic acid and methane. The catalyst obtained by microemulsion exhibited poor reproducibility. The catalyst synthesized by SFD achieved the largest CO2 conversion rate, a 30% higher than that obtained with the one synthesized by precipitation.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: One of the most promising technologies for the mitigation of CO2 emissions involves its electrocatalytic reduction to valuable products. However, the development of effective catalysts is still a challenge. In this work, three different techniques have been compared for the synthesis of catalysts involving Cu-based nanoparticles deposited on carbon nanotubes (Cu/CNT): precipitation, microemulsion and supercritical fluid deposition (SFD). According to XRD, SFD allows obtaining mainly copper nanoparticles, while copper oxides are obtained by precipitation. Crystallite size of predominant Cu species of catalysts are between 7 (microemulsion) and 16 nm (SFD). The use of these catalysts in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in gas phase produce carbon monoxide as main CO2 reduction product, followed by formic acid and methane. The catalyst obtained by microemulsion exhibited poor reproducibility. The catalyst synthesized by SFD achieved the largest CO2 conversion rate, a 30% higher than that obtained with the one synthesized by precipitation.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide emissions have become an important environmental problem in our days, mainly due to the use of fossil fuels for transport and electricity production, together with industry emissions, deforestation and agriculture. Nevertheless, predictions of international energy organizations point out that fossil fuels are going to be the main source of energy in the next years, even in a “sustainable development scenario” which considers an approach where the agreed objectives in terms of climate change, air quality and access to modern energy would be attained [1]. In this context, one of the measures to mitigate CO2 emissions is related to its capture and recycling, either through its use in processes (as solvent) or through its conversion to fuels and/or value-added products [2,3]. The electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 has received increasing attention in the last years, since it has a huge potential in the use of surplus electricity from renewable sources Jo ur na l P
re -p

for the conversion of CO2 to electro-fuels, which have bigger energy capacity storage than batteries [4]. Nowadays, the main challenges to achieve the implementation of the process are related to the development of effective, selective and stable electrocatalysts for the conversion of CO2, as well as the development of appropriate electrocatalytic cell design [5]. In this sense, many works in the literature study the use of different catalytic materials. Among the heterogeneous electrocatalysts outstand those based in metals such as Cu, Ag or Au, combined or not with carbon-based supports [6,7]. Thus, product selectivity depends mainly on the electrode (electrocatalyst) and the electrolyte (and therefore on the cell configuration). In general, it is known that Au and Ag electrocatalysts promote the conversion of CO2 to CO [5,8], whereas Cu favors the formation of hydrocarbons such as methane or ethylene [9–11]. However, functionalization of the electrodes allows tuning of the selectivity [4]. On the other hand, electrocatalysts based on earth abundant elements such as carbon, nitrogen and non-noble metals are especially interesting alternative for CO2 electroreduction [12]. In this context, catalysts involving Fe and Cu particles deposited on carbon supports (doped or undoped with nitrogen) are being studied [13,14]. As well, some works point out the important role of metal nanoparticles (Cu) on the electrocatalytic activity and selectivity for CO2 reduction reaction versus the use of metal foils as electrodes [9,15,16]. It should be noted that, according to the literature, the synthesis method used to prepare the electrocatalysts has an important effect on their catalytic activity given that the properties of the material obtained, such as particle size distribution, morphology, structure and composition depend on the synthesis technique [17,18]. Focusing on the catalysts based on metallic nanoparticles deposited on carbon supports, a wide variety of Jo ur na l P re -p r f
synthesis techniques can be considered. Among the conventional methods are incipient wetness impregnation, precipitation, chemical vapor deposition and flame spray pyrolysis [19]. The main disadvantages of incipient wetness impregnation rely on the obtention of particles with broad particle size distribution and on the use of large volumes of solvent. On the other hand, precipitation methods suffer from the lack of homogeneity of particle size distribution of the synthesized products. Chemical vapor deposition is the most common method for deposition of metal nanoparticles on different supports [20], and it requires high temperatures and extremely volatile precursors (toxic compounds in many cases). The main concern of this technique is related to kinetic limitations due to slow mass transfer in the nearness of the support. Flame spray pyrolysis method involves the use of liquid solutions with inorganic precursors and high temperatures to achieve their reduction, nevertheless, these conditions can lead to unwanted compounds. The sol-gel techniques have the advantage of being able to deposit nanoparticles on a support in a single step, but they can suffer the interference of the precursors due to polymerization processes that can give rise to undesired properties of the catalysts [19]. Another approach to carry out the formation of metal nanoparticles is the reverse micelle encapsulation or microemulsion method. It consists of the formation of microemulsions using two immiscible liquids and at least one surfactant, creating spheres that encapsulate a small amount of aqueous solution [18]. This method allows adjusting the size of the resulting nanoparticles (by using different surfactants), however, it has the drawback of possible interferences of remaining surfactant, or the need of methods such as oxygen plasma etching [9] to ensure surfactant elimination. Other techniques used in the synthesis of metal nanoparticles are spray deposition, thermal evaporation or electrodeposition, which have disadvantages related to the poor dispersion of the nanoparticles obtained, the presence of impurities from the precursors Jo ur n l P r -p r f
or the agglomeration of the nanoparticles, giving rise to poor control of their size and shape [21]. In this context, supercritical fluid deposition technique is becoming very attractive since it can offer several advantages of the conventional synthesis methods, especially when it is carried out using supercritical CO2 as reaction medium. This technique is relatively new, respectful with the environment and an efficient method to prepare homogeneously dispersed nanoparticles compared to other techniques [21]. The values of density of supercritical CO2 are similar to those of a liquid, allowing to dissolve concentrations of precursor up to three times higher than those typical of chemical vapor deposition processes [19]. In addition, the density and therefore the solvent power of supercritical CO2 can be modulated with changes in the temperature and pressure. This fact together with low viscosity values (like those of gases) favor rapid mass transfer in supercritical medium, leading to fast deposition rates. As well, supercritical fluids are characterized with low surface tension and complete miscibility with reacting gases (H2 or O2), what facilitate the contact between the support, the precursor and the reactants to form metal nanoparticles. This is especially interesting in case of porous supports such as nanotubes or aerogels where surface tension of liquid solvents difficult its diffusion through the pores. For all these reasons, supercritical fluid deposition is an interesting method to synthesize electrocatalysts consisting of metal nanoparticles deposited on carbon supports [22–25] to use them in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 [26,27]. Regarding the electrocatalytic cell design for CO2 reduction, it must be noticed that the conventional electrochemical cell configuration with CO2 dissolved in a liquid electrolyte has limitations related to the low solubility of CO2 in aqueous solutions, and its equilibrium with carbonic acid/bicarbonate/carbonate, being these species more difficult to reduce than CO2 [28]. Thus, although most works carried out up to now have studied Jo ur al Pr epr oo f
the electrochemical reduction of CO2 dissolved in aqueous electrolytes [4,6,8,9,15,16,29], it is necessary to design practical electrolyzes which can overcome these limitations [5]. In this sense, the approach of feeding CO2 in the gas phase to the cathodic compartment of the electrocatalytic cell along with the use of gas diffusion electrodes (GDE) such as those typical in PEM (polymer electrolyte membrane) fuel cells is a promising perspective [30]. GDE contain an electrically conductive catalyst and a gas/liquid/solid interface, whose objective is to alleviate the limitations of mass-transfer towards the surface of the catalyst. They commonly involve a reaction layer (mixture of catalyst particles and a carbonaceous support) and a gas diffusion layer (mixture of hydrophobic carbon black and a Teflon dispersion). An interesting configuration for CO2 reduction in the gas phase comprises the assembly of a set of two GDE (anode and cathode) to both sides of a solid polymer electrolyte such as an ion-conducting polymer able to transport H+ or OH- through (between the GDE). Taking all of this into account, the aim of this work has been to compare the electrocatalytic activity for CO2 electroreduction of three catalysts obtained by different synthesis methods. The electrocatalysts consisted of Cu nanoparticles deposited on commercial carbon nanotubes (Cu/CNT). The three synthesis methods used to obtain these materials have been precipitation, microemulsion (also known as inverse micelle encapsulation) and supercritical fluid deposition under experimental conditions previously used by several authors in literature to maximize the amount of metal deposited on the carbon support. The catalysts obtained have been characterized in order to know their metal concentration, the crystallinity of metal species deposited, the distribution of Cu-based nanoparticles size, as well as the deposition yield attained by each synthesis method. The catalytic activity of Cu/CNT synthesized by the three methods has been compared by analyzing the products obtained during the Jo ur n l P re -p r of
electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in the gas phase using a PEM type cell. The GDE of the cell (anode and cathode) comprised Cu/CNT spread on carbon paper, which were assembled to both sides of a proton exchange membrane. To our knowledge, the comparison of the activity of Cu/CNT obtained by different synthesis methods (including supercritical fluid deposition) has not been reported before for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2.

The experimental set-up used to synthesize the Cu/CNT catalyst using the supercritical technology (Cu/CNTsc) has been described elsewhere [26,27]. It consists of a PEM type electrochemical single cell (PaxiTech supplied by MICROBEAM, electrode geometric area: 25 cm2) with two compartments divided by a Nafion® 117 membrane. Finally, H2 (5 %) is added to the system to produce the reduction of the precursor to metallic copper at 400 ºC for 3 h. The solid sample obtained from the reactor (Cu/CNTpp catalyst) is then stored in a conveniently covered glass vial until its analysis or its use as electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: 2.3.3. Synthesis of Cu/CNT catalyst using supercritical CO2
sections.text:
The experimental procedure for the synthesis of Cu/CNTsc catalyst was previously described in several works of our group for Pt and Pb [26,27]. A typical synthesis experiment starts with the load of 0.25 g of metal precursor (copper acetylacetonate, 98 %, ACROS ORGANICS), 0.25 g of carbon nanotubes and 5 ml of methanol. Then, the metal precursor is dissolved in supercritical CO2 at 200 bar and 100 ºC for 1 hour under magnetic stirring. Then, hydrogen (4.5% volume) is introduced inside the reactor and pressure is increased with CO2 up to 250 bar for 30 minutes to reduce metal precursor to its metallic form. After that, the system is allowed to cool down and slowly depressurized, and then the solid is recovered with acetone from the reactor. Finally, the suspension obtained is vacuum filtered (0.45 µm Nylon) and the solid is dried in an oven at 40 ºC for 24 hours. The solid sample obtained from the filter (Cu/CNTsc catalyst) is then stored in a conveniently covered glass vial until its analysis or its use as electrocatalysts. It must be noted that the Cu/CNT catalysts synthetized by the three methods have not been preserved under inert atmosphere.

Taking into account the different analysis done, it can be concluded that the three synthesis methods studied allow obtaining very small copper-based nanoparticles deposited on the carbon nanotubes and, even, inside them. sections.heading: 3.2. CO2 electroreduction

As mentioned before, the electrocatalytic activity for CO2 reduction of the three catalysts synthesized has been studied. For that purpose, these materials have been used to make the GDE (anode and cathode) of a PEM type cell. Their activity has been evaluated by galvanostatic experiments, in terms of carbon dioxide conversion rate and CO2 reduction products distribution. Results showed correspond with the average values obtained from four replications of the experiments.
In addition to CO2 electroreduction galvanostatic experiments, linear sweep voltammetries have been carried out, by registering current intensity vs cell potential. It has been seen that Cu/CNTpp and Cu/CNTme lead to lower current densities than Cu/CNTsc for cell voltages above 2.9 V, and that this trend is more noticeable as the voltage increases. These results indicate that the catalyst synthesized by SFD (Cu/CNTsc) has better electrochemical behaviour than those obtained by precipitation and microemulsion methods (Figure S1 in Supplementary information). Therefore, Cu/CNTsc could be expected to be more active in CO2 conversion. However, it is difficult to distinguish between the current density due to CO2 reduction and H2O reduction, its competing reaction. Thus, to it is necessary to quantify the reduction products to determine the activity of these catalysts.

According to previous tests, the experimental error in results associated to CO2 electroreduction experiments in the PEM type cell is below 15 %. It is the case of results obtained with Cu/CNTsc, which exhibits the highest reproducibility among the three catalysts studied with deviation around 11 %. On the contrary, it can be observed in Table 3 that the standard deviation of CO2 conversion rates of the replicates carried out with Cu/CNTpp and Cu/CNTme are higher, it is around 25 % of the mean value with Cu/CNTpp and near 40 % of the mean value with Cu/CNTme catalyst. The lower reproducibility observed in these cases could be attributed to the behaviour of these catalysts.
To show the performance of these catalysts throughout the experiments, Figure S3 (in Supplementary information) shows the CO2 conversion rate obtained in each of the four replicates of the continuous electroreduction experiments carried out with the catalysts. In this context, Figure S4 (from Supplementary information) shows the steady-state cell voltage on each replicate, which also fluctuates around the average value. In both cases, CO2 conversion rate and steady-state voltage, the catalyst which behaves with the least variability throughout the experiments is Cu/CNTsc. This stable behaviour of Cu/CNTsc has also been observed in one of our previous works [47].
The results of CO2 conversion rate of the three catalysts could be attributed to the different oxidation state of the copper nanoparticles deposited on the carbon nanotubes according to Velasco-Vélez et al., 2019 [29], which investigated the CO2 reduction activity of Cu 0, Cu+ and Cu2+-like electrodes. According to their results, Cu0 and Cu+-like electrodes achieve a larger current efficiency in the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide than those formed by Cu2+-like catalysts. This hypothesis is in accordance to the XRD patterns previously commented in which metallic Cu0 and Cu+-like species were mainly observed in Cu/CNTsc while copper oxides (Cu +-like and Cu2+-like species) were mainly observed in the catalysts synthesized by precipitation and microemulsion methods. Moreover, there were some other copper species (such as Cu(NO3)2 and/or Cu2(OH)3(NO3)) different from Cu or copper oxides in Cu/CNTme. These species together with other factors such as a possible insufficient disaggregation of particles in Cu/CNTpp and Cu/CNTme catalysts that would cause less accessible Cu-based nanoparticles, should be responsible for the worse performance of these catalysts in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. Apart from all the above, it is relevant to note that the CO2 conversion rates obtained with Cu/CNT electrocatalysts tested in this work are between twelve and fifteen times higher than those obtained in experiments carried out using commercial CNT (without copper deposited). As well, the group of Professor Irabien studied the use of commercial Cu nanoparticles (60-80 nm) as electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction in the gas phase, attaining CO2 conversion rates similar to those reported in this work [51]. Otherwise, Cu/CNT catalysts have been used in the gas phase electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in fuel-cell-like reactors, using proton-exchange and alkaline anion-exchange membrane configurations (PEM and AAEM, respectively) [52]. These authors obtained Cu nanoparticles (50 nm) by microwave treatment followed by thermal reduction. They reported a maximum CO2 conversion rate when using AAEM very similar to that obtained by Cu/CNTsc in this work, whereas no CO2 conversion was observed with their PEM reactor. Thus, it can be affirmed that the electrocatalysts tested in this work, and especially that obtained by supercritical fluid deposition, present very interesting catalytic activity for CO2 conversion in the gas phase. Regarding the products obtained during the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction experiments, Figure 6 shows the formation rate of products observed when using the three catalysts synthesized in this work. In every case, the CO2 reduction products observed have been carbon monoxide, formic acid, methane, methanol, acetone and, in some cases, ipropanol. Hydrogen (from water reduction) has been also obtained in every case. Nevertheless, we focused our study on the carbon dioxide reduction products.

It can be observed that for every catalyst studied the main CO2 reduction product is carbon monoxide, the second formic acid and then methane. A low amount of methanol and acetone are obtained. Ethanol is produced with Cu/CNTsc and Cu/CNTme catalysts and ipropanol with the Cu/CNTme one. It must be marked that i-propanol has been observed in two of the four replicates carried out with Cu/CNTme catalyst leading to the high standard deviation observed with this product. Many works have reported methane as main reaction product and copper as the unique metal capable of converting carbon dioxide into hydrocarbons with good faradaic efficiency [51,53,54]. [53,54], CO2 can produce two different reaction intermediates depending on the metal used: CO2H* which is desorbed to HCOOH; and CO* which can be desorbed to CO or hydrogenated into COH* which can finally form methane, but also methanol and many other hydrocarbons. In this sense, Raciti and Wang [53] affirm that “Cu is distinct from the other metals by having an intermediate binding strength to CO*, achieving a balance of the barriers for activation of CO2 and hydrogenation of CO*”. That would be reason why Cu is able to convert CO2 into methane and other hydrocarbons. Nevertheless, in this work the main reduction product observed has been carbon monoxide instead of methane or ethylene reported in literature [6,29,53,54]. The behaviour observed with the Cu/CNT catalysts studied in this work could be attributed to the low size of the copper-based nanoparticles produced with the three methods used, which are below 20 nm. In this sense, Reske et al. [9] compared the activity of copper nanoparticles between 2 and 15 nm with that of a copper foil. They reported the conversion of CO2 to CO to the detriment of methane formation with Cu nanoparticles in the range studied (2-15 nm), as we have observed using the electrocatalysts synthesized in this work (Cu/CNT). On the other hand, it is important to note that other works in which copper nanoparticles have been used for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in gas phase also report the formation of CO as main CO2 reduction product. Wang et al. observed the formation of CO [52], and Merino-Garcia et al. reported the formation of CO followed by methane [51]. In this context, it is possible that other phenomena occurring in the cathodic CO2 gas-phase compartment limit the further reduction of CO to methane or other hydrocarbons. Thus, this behaviour could be promoted by a lack of protons on the cathode in the PEM type cell, due to their recombination with OH- produced by H2O reduction reaction [47]. Jo ur n l P r -p ro f
Regarding the comparison of the catalysts synthesized, the larger carbon monoxide and methane production have been obtained with the CuCNTsc catalyst which also shows the lowest dispersion (lowest standard deviation) for the CO production. On the other hand, Cu/CNTme catalyst shows the largest formation rate of formic acid. In short, the results obtained confirm that the catalyst synthesized in supercritical medium presents the best catalytic activity towards the conversion of CO2 among the three tested. This could be mainly attributed to the formation of Cu and Cu2O in Cu/CNTsc, the absence of copper species different from Cu and Cu oxides, and a good disaggregation of particles that could favour the accessibility to Cu-based nanoparticles. The results of the conversion rate of CO2 attained using this catalyst (Cu/CNTsc) in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in gas phase are comparable and, in some cases, superior to those reported in literature, pointing out its useful properties in terms of catalytic activity and conductivity. However, it must be noted that the Faradaic efficiencies (FE) attained in this work are very low, around 1 % (see Table S4). This fact could be largely attributed to the configuration of the electrochemical cell [55], whose design do not seem to be optimal to achieve high current efficiencies in CO2 electroreduction.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
The three synthesis methods studied in this work allow attaining Cu-based nanoparticles deposited on CNT with deposition yields of 60% for Cu/CNTme, 85% for Cu/CNTsc and 90% for Cu/CNTpp catalysts. XRD show that metallic copper nanoparticles are only attained with the supercritical CO2 deposition method, whereas with precipitation method mixed copper oxides are formed. In the case of microemulsion method, peaks corresponding to Cu(NO3)2 and/or Cu2(OH)3(NO3) have been also detected apart from CuO. Regarding the use of these catalysts in the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide in gas phase, CO has been the main CO2 reduction product observed in every case, followed by formic acid and methane. In terms of CO2 conversion rate, the catalyst obtained by precipitation synthesis achieved the lowest rate, whereas the one obtained by supercritical fluid deposition attained the highest. The comparison of the results attained with those reported in literature point out the great potential of supercritical fluid deposition technique in the development of electrocatalysts. These results together with the fact that supercritical fluid deposition is an environmentally friendly technique makes this technology a very promising one in the synthesis of advanced catalysts for environmental applications.
